mappings.note: Predicts the observable result of zinc in iron(II) sulphate and demands the equation - LO-2's 'uses the reactivity series to predict displacement reactions' clause verbatim. C 8.2-LO-2 was rejected because nothing is designed and no variable is controlled.

The selector is a phenomenon (the metal starts floating) and the explanation is adhering hydrogen bubbles - a single-metal observation, so LO-1. Contrast the 'name the metals that catch fire in water' item, where the selector is extremity of reactivity and the code is LO-2.

Amphoterism as the exception to 'metal oxides are basic' - LO-1's chemical-property clause. DEFECT: the stem asks for reactions with an acid and a base, but the stored answer stops after naming Al2O3, so the item is only half keyed.
Asks explicitly for a metal/non-metal verdict with justification from the basic oxide - the classification demand of LO-1.
The reactivity band is given in the stem; the work is listing observations (heat, floating). That makes it an observed-property item under LO-1 rather than a ranking item under LO-2.

Both parts are comparisons: selecting the metal that reacts only with steam, and explaining why sodium's hydrogen ignites while calcium's does not. Both need the series, so LO-2. DEFECT: sub-part (a)(ii) is stored as '[second case not printed]' although the key answers it with 'Copper'.

Genuinely two-part: (a) the high melting point of sodium chloride is an ionic-compound property, which only the competency reaches, while (b) non-metals failing to displace hydrogen is a metal/non-metal chemical contrast under LO-1.
Full extraction route for a low-reactivity metal from its sulphide ore, roasting then thermal decomposition, with equations - LO-6's core content.
Sacrificial or cathodic protection - a prevention method under LO-7, and specifically the one that is not a coating, which is what the stem asks for.

Two corrosion items: blackening in air and aluminium's protective oxide. DEFECT: part (i) reads 'Silver chloride becomes black', and the key explains it by reaction with sulphur to give silver sulphide; that chemistry belongs to silver metal, not to silver chloride, which darkens by photodecomposition.

WEAK FIT. Alloy constituents and uses, cited to LO-7 as the only outcome naming alloying. DEFECT: the key gives bronze as copper + zinc, which is brass; an MCQ earlier in this same chapter correctly keys bronze as copper + tin.

WEAK FIT. How alloy properties differ from those of the constituent metals. Only the corrosion-resistance half falls inside LO-7; hardness, strength, melting point, malleability and conductivity of alloys have no outcome anywhere in this frame.
The metal is named in the stem and the demand is to explain its storage from its own reaction with air and moisture - LO-1 under the name-given-explain split, not a ranking item.
Both parts are corrosion: aluminium's protective oxide and copper's green carbonate in damp air. LO-7 covers the mechanism and the resistance together.

Aluminium reacting with an alkali is amphoteric behaviour, a chemical-property exception used in the metal/non-metal classification (LO-1). It is not corrosion of a structure, so LO-7 does not apply despite the container framing.
Electron-dot structures and the transfer forming magnesium chloride. Bond formation from valence electrons is named only in the competency text; no learning outcome in this frame covers it.
Both parts are pairwise reactivity comparisons - silver against copper for the storage vessels, zinc against tin for the cans. LO-2 throughout; no corrosion product or prevention method is asked for.
One named metal burning in air, with the product and its physical state. Single-substance chemical property (LO-1).

Four-part item on the bond type and the resulting compound's melting point, solubility and conductivity. Every part concerns the ionic compound, which no learning outcome reaches, so the competency is cited.
The self-limiting oxide film that stops further oxidation - corrosion resistance under LO-7. Near-duplicate of an earlier item in this chapter and it honestly takes the same code.
Defines galvanisation and its purpose. LO-7 names galvanisation explicitly, so this is the tightest fit in the whole chapter.

A metal giving hydrogen with both an acid and a base is amphoteric behaviour plus the metal+acid class property - LO-1. The pop test is a one-line confirmation, not the apparatus-and-technique demand that earned C 8.2 on the gas-collection item.

Identifies magnesium from burning in air and demands the equation. LO-1 covers metal + oxygen as a class property; note the oxidation/reduction justification in part (c) is redox vocabulary that no outcome in this frame covers.
A three-metal comparison of reactivity with cold and hot water, which is LO-2's ordering clause. 'In tabular form' is a presentation instruction, not an inquiry design, so C 8.2 is not co-cited.
Lists the physical properties of metals - the property inventory LO-1 asks students to classify from.
